Using APIs and Web Scraping with R

Building a GOV.UK corpus

Objective

In this tutorial we will learn how to use an API with R and how to combine API access with web scraping.

We will use the public GOV.UK Search API to:

  1. search for government press releases;
  2. retrieve structured metadata;
  3. turn the API response into a dataframe (table);
  4. understand pagination and query parameters;
  5. obtain the URL of each document;
  6. scrape the full text of selected documents;
  7. save the result as a corpus for qualitative analysis.

R, RStudio and Posit Cloud

R and RStudio

But, first, the very basic.

R is a programming language for data analysis, statistics and scientific computing. It is free, open source and works on Windows, macOS and Linux.

RStudio is an Integrated Development Environment (IDE). It provides an interface for writing, running and organizing R code.

R is the language. RStudio is the environment we use to work with that language.

Instead of installing R and RStudio on your computer, you can use Posit Cloud in a web browser:

https://posit.cloud/

Create an account and then choose:

New Project → New RStudio Project

This opens the RStudio IDE in your browser.

RStudio is usually divided into four panels:

Panel Main use
Source Write and save code
Console Execute commands and see results
Environment See objects currently stored in memory
Output Files, plots, packages, help and other outputs

For this tutorial, we will mainly work in the Source and Console panels.

You can type commands directly into the Console, but for research it is better to save your code in a script or an R Markdown document.

To create a script:

File → New File → R Script

To execute one line of R code, place the cursor on that line and press:

Ctrl + Enter

on Windows/Linux, or:

Cmd + Enter

on macOS.

A few basic R concepts

R allows us to store values in objects using the assignment operator <-.

x <- 10
name <- "GOV.UK"

x
## [1] 10
name
## [1] "GOV.UK"

Objects appear in the Environment panel.

A dataframe is a rectangular data structure: rows usually represent cases and columns represent variables.

example_data <- data.frame(
  id = 1:3,
  title = c("Document A", "Document B", "Document C")
)

example_data
##   id      title
## 1  1 Document A
## 2  2 Document B
## 3  3 Document C

Our goal is to build a dataframe in which each row is one GOV.UK document.

Functions perform operations. A function usually has the form:

function_name(argument1, argument2)

For example:

mean(c(10, 20, 30))
## [1] 20

R includes many functions by default, but packages add additional tools.

We will use three packages:

  • tidyverse for data manipulation;
  • httr2 for interacting with APIs;
  • rvest for web scraping.

Install them once in your Posit Cloud project:

install.packages(c("tidyverse", "httr2", "rvest"))

Then load them every time you start a new R session:

library(tidyverse)
library(httr2)
library(rvest)

What is an API?

API stands for Application Programming Interface.

An API allows one computer program to request information from another program or service in a structured way.

When we browse a website, a server usually sends us HTML designed to be displayed in a browser.

When we use an API, the server usually sends us structured data designed to be processed by software.

An endpoint is the web address where we send the request.

The public GOV.UK Search API endpoint is:

https://www.gov.uk/api/search.json

APIs often allow us to modify a request using parameters.

A URL might look conceptually like this:

https://example.org/api?q=artificial+intelligence&count=20

The ? begins the query parameters.

The & separates different parameters.

Here:

  • q contains the search query;
  • count defines how many results we want.

The most common operation for retrieving public information is a GET request.

In this tutorial we only need GET requests: we are asking GOV.UK to return information. We are not modifying anything on its servers.

Many APIs return data in JSON format.

JSON represents information using objects, fields and values.

For example:

{
  "title": "Example document",
  "date": "2026-01-01",
  "url": "/government/news/example"
}

This is convenient because R can convert JSON into lists and dataframes.

Searching in the GOV.UK API

GOV.UK provides a public search endpoint:

https://www.gov.uk/api/search.json

Documentation:

https://docs.publishing.service.gov.uk/repos/search-api/using-the-search-api.html

The API allows us to search and filter documents by several fields.

Some useful parameters are:

Parameter Meaning
q Search terms
count Number of results
start Starting position, used for pagination
fields Fields we want returned
filter_content_store_document_type Document type
filter_public_timestamp Publication date
filter_organisations Organisation
order Sort order

For our example, we will search for GOV.UK press releases mentioning artificial intelligence.

Our first API request

We begin by defining the endpoint.

api <- "https://www.gov.uk/api/search.json"

Now we build a request.

request_govuk <- request(api) |>
  req_url_query(
    q = "artificial intelligence",
    filter_content_store_document_type = "press_release",
    filter_public_timestamp = "from:2024-01-01,to:2026-09-30",
    count = 20,
    fields = "title,description,link,public_timestamp"
  )

At this point we have constructed the request, but we have not sent it yet.

We can inspect it:

request_govuk |>
  req_dry_run()

Now we send it.

response <- request_govuk |>
  req_perform()

HTTP responses have status codes.

Some common examples are:

Code Meaning
200 Request successful
404 Resource not found
422 The server understood the request but one or more parameters are invalid
429 Too many requests

Check the status of our request:

resp_status(response)
## [1] 200

If everything worked, the result should be 200.

The response body contains JSON.

We can ask httr2 to convert it into an R object:

data <- response |>
  resp_body_json(simplifyVector = TRUE)

Inspect the top-level elements:

names(data)
## [1] "results"                "total"                 
## [3] "start"                  "aggregates"            
## [5] "suggested_queries"      "suggested_autocomplete"
## [7] "es_cluster"

The API response includes information about the search as well as the actual documents.

Check the total number of matches:

data$total
## [1] 597

Now inspect the results:

head(data$results)

The API returns relative GOV.UK links, so we create complete URLs.

documents <- documents |>
  mutate(
    url = paste0("https://www.gov.uk", link),
    date = as.Date(substr(public_timestamp, 1, 10))
  )

Keep the main variables:

documents <- documents |>
  select(title, description, date, url)

We now have the beginning of a research corpus: one row per document and one column per piece of metadata.

What is Web scraping?

At this point we have obtained structured metadata from the API.

But we may still want the full text of each press release.

This introduces a second technique: web scraping.

The distinction is important:

API access Web scraping
Requests structured data from an endpoint Reads content from a webpage
Usually returns JSON Usually reads HTML
Fields are explicitly defined We identify HTML elements ourselves
Usually more stable Can break if the website design changes
Best option when the required data are available Useful when information exists only in the webpage

Web scraping means automatically retrieving information from webpages.

A webpage is written in HTML.

A simplified page might look like this:

<html>
  <body>
    <h1>Press release title</h1>
    <div class="article">
      <p>First paragraph.</p>
      <p>Second paragraph.</p>
    </div>
  </body>
</html>

The browser transforms this HTML into the page we see.

With web scraping, we work in the opposite direction: we read the HTML and select the elements that contain the information we need.

A few basic notions of HTML

HTML is organized into elements such as:

  • h1: main heading;
  • h2: secondary heading;
  • p: paragraph;
  • a: link;
  • div: container.

Elements can also have attributes such as:

<div class="article">

The class is article.

CSS selectors allow us to identify elements.

For example:

h1

selects <h1> elements.

.article

selects elements with class article.

main .govspeak

selects elements with class govspeak that appear inside the main section of the page.

A useful way to identify selectors is to open the browser’s developer tools and use Inspect on the element of interest.

Our first web scraping

Reading one webpage with rvest

Take the URL of one document from our API results.

example_url <- documents$url[1]

example_url
## [1] "https://www.gov.uk/government/news/joint-declaration-of-intent-between-the-united-kingdom-of-great-britain-and-northern-ireland-and-ukraine-on-a-uk-ukraine-artificial-intelligence-partn"

Read the HTML:

page <- read_html(example_url)

Extract the main heading:

page |>
  html_element("h1") |>
  html_text2()
## [1] "Joint Declaration of Intent between the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and Ukraine on a UK-Ukraine Artificial Intelligence Partnership"

For many GOV.UK press releases, the main text is rendered inside elements using the govspeak class.

page |>
  html_elements("main .govspeak") |>
  html_text2()
## [1] "We, the President of Ukraine and the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, meeting at a decisive moment for European security, and united in our resolve to shape the transformation of modern warfare,\n\nACKNOWLEDGING the profound impact of artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, and network-enabled capability, and the strategic imperative for our two nations to lead in the safe, responsible, and operationally decisive application of Defence AI,\n\nRESOLVED that the technological edge of democracies must be preserved as a foundation of deterrence;\n\nRECOGNISING that Ukraine’s defence, resilience, and unparalleled operational experience represent a crucial contribution not only to its own sovereignty and territorial integrity, but also to the stability and security of the eastern flank of Europe, NATO, and the Euro-Atlantic community,\n\nRECALLING the existing framework of bilateral commitments between our two nations, in particular the 100-Year Partnership Agreement and the Agreement on Security Co-operation,\n\nDETERMINED that the United Kingdom and Ukraine should advance together — combining Ukraine’s unrivalled battlefield experience with the United Kingdom’s technological, industrial and research strength to build the AI-era armed forces our two nations, and our allies, will depend on,\n\nAFFIRMING our shared and existing determination to deepen our defence partnership and jointly contribute to the development of future European defence capabilities,\n\nDeclare the following intent:\n\nI. Strategic Vision. We will act as close partners in developing next-generation, AI-enabled armed forces – leveraging our engineering, industry, academic capacity and defence organisations’ expertise to accelerate the development and deployment of AI-enabled military capabilities that strengthen Ukraine’s battlefield advantage and support the development of next-generation AI-driven Armed Forces powered by rapid innovation, autonomous systems, and network advantage.\n\nII. Cooperation Model. Our cooperation will proceed through three interlocking pillars: (1) Government-to-Government collaboration on co-developed models, secure data and compute pathways, and joint assurance; (2) Industry, coordinated through government-to-government arrangements to develop, test and deploy AI-enabled capabilities linked to agreed operational problem sets; and (3) Academia and Research, on autonomy, AI assurance, cyber security and synthetic data. Together, we will establish a model for developing and fielding AI-enabled military capabilities that others can follow.\n\nIII. Principles. Cooperation will respect the sovereignty of each Party’s assets and data; be underpinned by trusted safeguards on data, IP and export controls in line with the national legislation; combine agility with proportionate governance; and deliver mutual strategic benefit and NATO interoperability. By mutual agreement, we will extend the outputs of this Partnership to trusted allies and partners.\n\nIV. Leadership and Oversight. We will steward this Partnership at the highest political level, with senior Defence leads empowered to drive delivery in line with the mutually agreed objectives.\n\nV. Framework for Implementation. We resolve to proceed on a pilot-first basis, giving priority to practical cooperation already underway. Further arrangements will be brought forward within the next few months, ensuring that this Partnership takes a tangible form from the outset and moves at the pace that our shared security requires.\n\nThis Declaration reflects our shared political intent and does not create legally binding obligations."

Because a page can contain more than one matching element, we can collapse them into a single string.

text <- page |>
  html_elements("main .govspeak") |>
  html_text2() |>
  paste(collapse = "\n\n")

text

Important: HTML structures can change. A scraper depends on the structure of the website, so selectors should always be checked before collecting a large corpus.

We can turn the previous operations into a reusable function.

scrape_govuk_text <- function(url) {

  page <- read_html(url)

  page |>
    html_elements("main .govspeak") |>
    html_text2() |>
    paste(collapse = "\n\n")
}

Test it with one URL:

scrape_govuk_text(documents$url[1])

Scrape several documents

corpus <- documents |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

Now retrieve the text of each page.

corpus <- corpus |>
  mutate(
    text = map_chr(
      url,
      function(x) {
        Sys.sleep(0.2)
        scrape_govuk_text(x)
      }
    )
  )

map_chr() repeats the function once for every URL and returns a character vector.

Sys.sleep(0.2) introduces a short pause between requests. This is a simple way to avoid sending many requests to a website at the same instant.

Inspect and clean the corpus

Inspect the dataset:

corpus |>
  select(title, date, text)

We can remove unnecessary repeated whitespace:

corpus <- corpus |>
  mutate(
    text = str_squish(text)
  )

We can also calculate a simple word count:

corpus <- corpus |>
  mutate(
    words = str_count(text, "\\S+")
  )

Inspect document sizes:

corpus |>
  select(title, date, words) |>
  arrange(desc(words))

Save the corpus

Create a folder for data:

dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)

Save the dataframe as CSV:

write_csv(corpus, "data/govuk_ai_press_releases.csv")

You can later read it again with:

corpus <- read_csv("data/govuk_ai_press_releases.csv")

Good practices

When using APIs and web scraping in research:

  1. prefer an official API when one exists;
  2. document the endpoint and all parameters used;
  3. record the date when the data were collected;
  4. save the original URLs;
  5. avoid sending unnecessary requests;
  6. check the website’s conditions and technical restrictions;
  7. keep the raw corpus separate from later transformations;
  8. make corpus inclusion and exclusion criteria explicit;
  9. remember that websites and APIs can change over time.

Minimal complete workflow

library(tidyverse)
library(httr2)
library(rvest)

response <- request("https://www.gov.uk/api/search.json") |>
  req_url_query(
    q = "artificial intelligence",
    filter_content_store_document_type = "press_release",
    filter_public_timestamp = "from:2024-01-01,to:2026-09-30",
    count = 100,
    fields = "title,description,link,public_timestamp"
  ) |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_json(simplifyVector = TRUE)

documents <- response$results |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(
    url = paste0("https://www.gov.uk", link),
    date = as.Date(substr(public_timestamp, 1, 10))
  )

scrape_govuk_text <- function(url) {
  read_html(url) |>
    html_elements("main .govspeak") |>
    html_text2() |>
    paste(collapse = "\n\n")
}

corpus <- documents |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  mutate(
    text = map_chr(
      url,
      function(x) {
        Sys.sleep(0.2)
        print(x)
        scrape_govuk_text(x)
      }
    )
  )
